newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: GERMANY AIMING FOR MONETARY UNION, WAIGEL SAYS.
newsitem.headline: GERMANY AIMING FOR MONETARY UNION, WAIGEL SAYS.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Sunday Germany would do its utmost to qualify for a single European currency and reiterated the Maastricht convergence criteria would set the pace.

Waigel, on a brief visit to Vienna, said Germany would not seek special treatment from the European Union when it took a decision next year, based on 1997 economic data, on the founding members of the euro.

"We will do all we can to fulfil the convergence criteria in 1997. The convergence criteria will determine the timetable," Waigel told reporters after a meeting with Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima and Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger.

"We will stick to the criteria as they stand...The figures will remain as they were agreed in the Maastricht Treaty and there will be a narrow interpretation," he said, dismissing suggestions that Germany may go soft on the Maastricht rules.

In Germany's favour, Waigel pointed to rising investment and business confidence and real economic growth forecast at 2-1/2 percent this year. He said he hoped the labour market would pick up in March, easing unemployment that soared to a post-World War Two record last month.
But he noted Bonn had born immense costs in recent years from reunification, the rebuilding of central and eastern Europe and a wave of refugees from the former Yugoslavia.
Klima said he considered it crucial that Germany was part of the single currency from the start, scheduled for 1999.
"The deutschmark is a kind of anchor currency for many European countries. It is unimaginable to start EMU without Germany," he said.
Klima's Finance Minister Edlinger underlined his confidence that Austria would be among the first countries to introduce the euro.

"We can assume that Austria will reach the Maastricht criteria in a lasting way in 1997. Budget measures already in place should make it possible to meet the three percent budget deficit ceiling without another austerity budget," he said.

Austria's 1997 budget was designed to bring the budget deficit below the 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, set down in the Maastricht Treaty. Economists raised doubts last week, however, that central government would manage to stick to its spending target.
Klima warned it would be damaging for Austria if it failed to qualify for a single European currency that included Germany, its biggest trading partner.
"If Germany takes part in European Economic and Monetary Union it is vital Austria does the same," he said.
